abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel cognitive-affective theory for emotion recognition that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between physiological signals and emotional states. Traditional approaches treat emotion as discrete categorical labels mapped to physiological patterns, which oversimplifies the inherently dynamic and dimensional nature of affective experience. We propose the Dynamic Affective State Transition (DAST) framework, which models emotions as trajectories through a continuous multidimensional space rather than static points. The theoretical contribution lies in introducing temporal dependency structures that capture how emotional states evolve and influence subsequent cognitive processing. We formalize this framework using probabilistic graphical models that incorporate both immediate physiological responses and longer-term emotional dynamics. Experimental validation on three benchmark datasets (DEAP, MAHNOB-HCI, and DREAMER) demonstrates that our paradigm shift enables superior prediction of emotional transitions compared to state-of-the-art classification methods. The DAST framework establishes new theoretical foundations for affective computing research, particularly for applications requiring understanding of emotional evolution in human-computer interaction scenarios.

This paper introduces an enhanced theoretical analysis of multimodal fusion strategies for affective computing, significantly advancing current understanding of how different data modalities interact during emotion recognition. While existing fusion approaches primarily focus on feature concatenation or late decision combination, we provide a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing intermediate fusion operations that preserve modality-specific temporal dependencies. Our theoretical contribution derives novel bounds on recognition performance that explicitly account for inter-modality correlation structures and their evolution during emotional episodes. We prove that optimal fusion occurs when the model architecture mirrors the causal relationship between physiological signals (cardiac, electrodermal, and neural responses) and observable emotional expressions. Building upon information-theoretic principles, we establish conditions under which multimodal analysis outperforms unimodal approaches, providing concrete guidance for system designers. Empirical verification on the ASCERTAIN dataset confirms our theoretical predictions, demonstrating up to 12.4% improvement in valence-arousal estimation accuracy compared to conventional fusion methods. This work provides both analytical tools and practical insights for advancing sentiment analysis in real-world applications.

We present EmoSync, a groundbreaking real-time affective human-computer interaction system that fundamentally transforms how computers perceive and respond to user emotional states. Unlike conventional systems that process each modality independently before combining results, EmoSync introduces a neurobiologically-inspired architecture where facial expression recognition, voice intonation analysis, and physiological signal processing occur through synchronized neural pathways that mirror human emotional perception. The system employs novel cross-modal attention mechanisms that dynamically weight input sources based on contextual relevance and signal reliability. For facial analysis, we developed a lightweight transformer architecture optimized for edge deployment, enabling privacy-preserving emotion recognition without cloud connectivity. The physiological processing module integrates wearable sensor data with computer vision-based remote photoplethysmography. Crucially, EmoSync generates adaptive system responses through an emotion-congruent feedback generator that modulates interaction modalities (visual, auditory, haptic) based on detected user affect. Deployment experiments across diverse HCI scenarios—including educational tutoring, therapeutic support, and collaborative work—demonstrate that EmoSync achieves 89.3% emotion recognition accuracy with sub-200ms latency while significantly improving user engagement and satisfaction metrics.

This paper introduces an improved system architecture for continuous mental state recognition in naturalistic settings, addressing critical limitations of existing approaches when deployed in real-world environments with uncontrolled conditions. Existing systems suffer from significant performance degradation due to demographic variations, environmental noise, and subject-specific physiological differences. Our Enhanced Continuous Affect Monitor (ECAM) advances the state-of-the-art through three key innovations: First, we developed a domain-adaptive feature normalization pipeline that automatically adjusts for individual baseline differences and environmental factors. Second, we designed a hierarchical attention network that progressively focuses on the most discriminative temporal segments and modality channels, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Third, we implemented a lightweight continual learning framework enabling the system to adapt to new users without catastrophic forgetting. The complete pipeline processes video, audio, and electrodermal activity in real-time, making it suitable for practical deployment in mental health monitoring and adaptive human-computer interaction applications. Extensive evaluation across four datasets with 847 participants demonstrates substantial improvements: 15.7% higher accuracy, 34% reduced latency, and significantly improved robustness to partial sensor failure. Case studies in workplace stress monitoring validate the system's utility for affective applications.
